character_and_relationship_context: Amina Adebayo lives in a rented room in Mushin, a dense Lagos neighborhood with the hum of generators and the first calls of street vendors. She wakes at 5 a.m., ties her wrapper tightly, grabs her short broom, and walks to a building site where she sweeps rubble for 500 naira. The work is not guaranteed from one day to the next, but today is secure. After work she counts the day’s earning twice before folding it into the pocket of her dress, then goes home to wash and change for a vocational carpentry course in the afternoon. In the carpentry class she is the only woman; she sits near the back, watches the instructor’s hands more than his words, and waits for the moment to ask a question she has already mentally rehearsed. She keeps a worn notebook recording every expense with precision: 50 naira for a sachet of water, 100 for a handful of groundnuts, 200 for a fresh notebook leaf; she applies the same precision to her measurements. Her tools—a hammer, a chisel, and a small saw—are kept in a locked metal box under her bed. She oils the hinges herself every Friday evening, a ritual her late father taught her before he died of a fever she never fully understood when she was twelve. Since then she has depended on the order she imposes: double-checking measurements before cutting, triple-checking the lock on the box, and counting each day’s coins in her palm until she can translate them into rent, food, or an extra lesson. She treats thrift as necessity rather than virtue. A tension is present: she wants to be generous and quietly slips an extra piece of maize to the neighbor’s child, but every kobo she gives feels like a loss against an uncertain future. Her faith is quiet and tight; she prays in the morning not for riches but for no accident on the site, no broken tool, and no sudden illness that would unravel the fragile architecture of her days. She speaks Yoruba with her landlady and Pidgin at the site, but writes in careful school-learned English in her notebook because she once heard that could open a door. She does not laugh easily, but when a fellow trainee, Emeka, taps his foot in rhythm without noticing, she smiles to herself briefly and returns to the grain of the wood under her palm. She will cut now and measure again afterwards, because caution is the only wealth she has ever reliably owned. Her mother lives in Ibadan and sends notes only for urgent family events; she expects Amina to maintain ties despite distance. Her aunt, her mother’s elder sister, values large family gatherings and will notice Amina’s absence. Emeka, the quiet older trainee, sometimes shares his offcuts with her and has become a silent ally in the workshop. When faced with competing obligations, Amina has previously skipped a family wedding to attend an extra carpentry session, then sent a small gift later. She regularly postpones minor purchases, such as replacing a worn sandal, to keep her tool fund intact.
objective_situation: After her morning sweep, Amina’s landlady stops her in the courtyard and holds out a folded note from Amina’s mother. The note announces that her cousin’s baby will be named next Saturday in Ibadan, and her aunt expects her to attend. The ceremony will last all day, and attendance would require missing her carpentry class and paying for transport. She has only a few days to reply. Her mother writes that she can borrow a lace blouse from her sister, but Amina knows her tools need oil that weekend and she cannot afford both the trip and a new chisel. She stands by the gate, the note in her hand, weighing the pull of family duty against the order of her workshop routine.
state_and_available_memories: She has just finished sweeping rubble and is breathing heavily; the morning heat already beads sweat on her forehead. Her hands are calloused and slightly sore from gripping the broom handle, and she is hungry, having eaten only a piece of leftover garri before dawn. Immediate memory: The note’s handwriting—her mother’s rounded letters—reminds her of the day her father died and her mother wrote the same careful script to tell the school she would not return. Immediate memory: The phrase 'naming ceremony' recalls her own first day at the carpentry class, when she introduced herself and no one replied. Reflective memory: She recalls her father oiling his tools every Friday and saying, 'A tool that is kept is a tool that lasts,' a phrase she repeats to herself before each weekend ritual. Reflective memory: She remembers attending her cousin’s wedding two years ago, where her mother whispered that family shows up even when the road is hard.
name: Amina Adebayo
